summary: Defines several structured syntax suffixes for media type names, namely +json, +ber, +der, +fastinfoset, +wbxml and +zip. A suffix tells software the underlying format, so generic tools can handle specialized types. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A label like cake with chocolate shows what is inside. These endings tell a computer the basic kind of a file, even when the file has a fancy name.

subtitle: Registers six more name suffixes, such as +json and +zip, that tell software what format a media type is built on.

tldr.problem: A specialized media type name does not say what underlying format its content uses, so generic software cannot tell it could parse the data as, say, plain JSON.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines and registers the +json, +ber, +der, +fastinfoset, +wbxml and +zip structured syntax suffixes, and gives the registration form for +xml, each with rules for encoding, fragment identifiers and security.
tldr.outcome: A media type ending in a registered suffix can be handled generically by receivers that do not need its special semantics. The RFC updates RFC 3023 and was itself updated by RFC 7303.

today: RFC 6839 is Informational. It updates RFC 3023 and has itself been updated by RFC 7303.

sections.title: Why Suffixes Exist
sections.content:
A media type name can carry partitioned meta-information as a suffix. RFC 3023 created the +xml suffix for media types whose content is XML underneath, meaning it could be parsed as application/xml as well as under its own type. RFC 6838 defines a Structured Syntax Suffix Registry for such suffixes.

Several suffixes were already in use in registrations: +json, +der, +fastinfoset and +wbxml. This document defines and registers those, adds +ber and +zip, and updates RFC 3023 so that +xml is formally registered under the RFC 6838 procedure.
sections.eli5: Many file types are really a special kind of a simpler type. A suffix is a tag at the end of the name that says which simple type it is built from.

sections.title: When to Use These Suffixes
sections.content:
Each suffix fits when the media type identifies the semantics of the payload, so that knowing the specific type allows more specific processing than generic handling of the underlying representation.

At the same time, the suffix lets a receiver do generic processing of the underlying format when two conditions hold: the receiver does not need to handle the particular semantics of the exact media type, and no special knowledge is needed to parse the underlying representation beyond what would be needed for any example of it.
sections.eli5: If a tool only needs to open the box and does not care what the toy inside is, the suffix tells it what kind of box to open.

sections.title: The Six New Suffix Definitions
sections.content:
Each suffix has a registration form. +json may be used with any type whose representation follows application/json (RFC 4627); JSON may be UTF-8, UTF-16 or UTF-32. +ber and +der cover the ITU Basic Encoding Rules and Distinguished Encoding Rules, both binary, and the text notes that the Expert Reviewer should understand the relationship between the two when choosing the proper suffix.

+fastinfoset covers the Fast Infoset binary representation of the XML Information Set, following application/fastinfoset. +wbxml covers WAP Binary XML, following application/vnd.wap.wbxml. +zip covers the ZIP file storage and transfer format, following application/zip, which is used as the underlying representation by a variety of file formats.

For all of them, the interoperability considerations are listed as not applicable, the contact is the Apps Area Working Group, and the IESG has change control.
sections.eli5: Six new endings were added to the list: one for JSON text, one each for two kinds of ASN.1 binary, one for compact binary XML, one for wireless-style binary XML, and one for zip files.

sections.title: Fragment Identifier Rules
sections.content:
Every registration gives the same layered rule for fragment identifiers on a specific type xxx/yyy+suffix. If the fragment is defined by the suffix and resolves under the suffix rules, process it as the suffix specifies. If it is defined by the suffix but does not resolve under those rules, process it as specified for xxx/yyy+suffix. If the suffix does not define it, process it as specified for xxx/yyy+suffix.

The suffix's own rules should follow those of the base type. At the time of publication no fragment syntax was defined for application/json, +ber, +der, application/fastinfoset, application/vnd.wap.wbxml or application/zip.
sections.eli5: When a link points to a spot inside a file, the suffix's rules are tried first, and if they do not cover that spot, the specific type's own rules decide.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and +xml
sections.content:
The IANA section points to the registration forms in Sections 3.1 to 3.6. It also supplies the registration for +xml, to reflect what RFC 3023 says, with the addition of fragment identifier considerations. XML is allowed in both 7-bit and 8-bit encodings; in UTF-8 it is 8bit compatible and in UTF-16 or UTF-32 it is binary.

The fragment rules for +xml follow application/xml, which at publication were defined in RFC 3023, Sections 5 and 7. The text notes that RFC 3023 was in the process of being updated by a separate XML media types document.
sections.eli5: The registry office gets a form for each new ending, and the old +xml ending gets its official form too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Each registration has its own security section, and each media type under a suffix can add more. For +ber and +der, the type-length-value structure makes it easy to build malicious content with invalid length fields that can cause buffer overruns, and arbitrary nesting may allow content that causes a stack overflow. Interpreters should guard against both. The text says there are no security considerations inherent in Fast Infoset or WBXML. For ZIP it notes the two forms of encryption it supports, Strong Encryption and AES at 128-bit, 192-bit and 256-bit.

The general warning is about changes. Because the generic fragment identifier rules take precedence over media-type-specific rules, updating a suffix registration or adding conflicting rules can break existing registrations and implementations, and can introduce interoperability and security issues. Care should be taken to review all previously registered types before updating a suffix.
sections.eli5: Some file kinds can be tricked with lying size numbers or boxes inside boxes, so programs reading them must be careful. Changing the rules later could also break files that already follow the old rules.
